children: Defense technology startup Covenant on Wednesday announced more than $250 million in funding and plans to begin large-scale production of a lower-cost, long-range missile system in early 2027.

The privately held company said its Anthem weapon is designed to carry heavy payloads over long distances while costing substantially less than comparable legacy systems. Covenant is pitching the missile as a response to concerns that modern conflicts can deplete precision-guided weapons faster than defense manufacturers can replace them.

Covenant has raised the funding across three rounds led by Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, Lux Capital, 8VC, Aleph and Lightspeed Venture Partners. The company did not disclose its valuation or detailed financial terms.
Production targeted for 2027

Covenant opened a 105,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in the Dallas area and expects serial production to begin in the first quarter of 2027. It plans to ramp up capacity to 5,000 units annually.
The company also operates a 110,000-square-foot facility in Saxony, Germany, supported by a European supply chain, and a 32,000-square-foot facility in northern Israel.
Anthem has completed more than 200 flights since its first flight in August 2025, Covenant said. Those flights included multiple tests with the U.S. Army in the United States and overseas.

Covenant did not disclose Anthem’s precise range, payload capacity or expected unit price. Those details would be important for comparing the system with existing long-range weapons and evaluating whether its planned production economics are achievable.
About $150 million in orders

The startup has booked approximately $150 million in orders, including research, qualification and production contracts. Covenant said it expects additional awards before the end of the year, although some customers restrict disclosure of their contracting activities.

The company is working with the U.S. Army under an Other Transaction Agreement for accelerated testing and qualification. It also has a contract with the U.S. Navy’s Rapid Capabilities Office to adapt the ground-launched missile into a “Maritime Anthem” variant.
That project is valued at roughly $70 million, includes a cost-sharing component and will fund modifications intended to make the weapon easier to export to U.S. allies and partners.
Designed for mass production

Covenant said most Anthem components are commercially available, while it has secured long-term agreements covering other critical parts. Its supply chain spans allied countries, an arrangement intended to reduce wartime production bottlenecks.

The missile is part of a broader system that includes transportation, storage, launch and reloading equipment. Covenant also developed its own mission-planning and command-and-control software to coordinate large-scale launches.

The design reflects growing investor and Pentagon interest in weapons that can be manufactured more quickly and in greater numbers than traditional missile systems. Defense startups increasingly argue that even highly advanced weapons provide limited deterrence if military inventories cannot support an extended conflict.

“We don’t lack advanced weapons, we lack enough of them, and that’s a production question as much as a technology one,” Mike Garcia, a former U.S. representative who advises Covenant, said in a statement.
Execution remains the test

For investors, Covenant’s disclosed order book, government contracts and manufacturing footprint provide evidence of early customer interest. Its prominent venture backers also give the company considerable financial resources as it moves toward production.

However, Anthem still must navigate qualification, manufacturing scale-up and government procurement processes. Covenant’s goal of producing thousands of missiles annually represents a significant jump from flight testing to high-volume manufacturing.

“Now the measure of our success is execution: delivering mission-critical capability to our customers on time, at scale, and with the performance they expect,” said Abby Denburg, Covenant’s president and chief growth officer.
Covenant is hiring for engineering, manufacturing and operations positions at its Texas facility.
